title: How 911 Figures Out Which Floor You're On #shorts
summary: FCC rules require height within 3 meters for 80% of indoor wireless 911 calls in the biggest markets; phones use pressure sensors, but no database reliably turns height into a floor.
sources: Consumers make 240 million calls to 911 each year, and in many areas 80% or more are from wireless phones; z-axis (vertical) accuracy of plus or minus 3 meters for 80% of indoor wireless E911 calls, in the top 25 markets by 3 Apr 2021 and the top 50 by 3 Apr 2023; nearly all smartphones appear to have barometric pressure sensors; it is not now technically feasible to reliably convert z-axis data to a floor level and no authoritative floor database exists; dispatchable location = street address, floor level and office or apartment number (FCC Fifth Report and Order, Wireless E911 Location Accuracy Requirements, Federal Register, 16 Jan 2020): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2020-01-16/html/2019-28483.htm
Pressure decreases with height (US National Weather Service, pressure training page): https://www.weather.gov/source/zhu/ZHU_Training_Page/winds/pressure_winds/Pressure.htm

scenes.narration: {911|Nine one one} location rules now include height: within {3|three} meters for {80%|eighty percent} of indoor calls.
How? Nearly all smartphones carry a pressure sensor, and air pressure drops as you go up.
But a height isn't a floor. In {2019|twenty nineteen}, the FCC found no database that could reliably convert one to the other.
So the rules also accept a dispatchable location: street address, floor and apartment.
